title: ‘It beggars belief’ as DWP ‘drags its heels’ over subpostmaster prosecutions reviews
raw_text:
The Department of Work & Pensions (DWP) has not yet appointed an independent reviewer of its prosecutions of subpostmasters or signed off terms of reference, almost 18 months after the review was announced.

Campaigning peers said it is time for Parliament “to step in” and that “something is very wrong at the heart of the government”, while a lawyer representing subpostmasters said the delay “beggars belief”.

In the aftermath of the Post Office Horizon scandal hitting the headlines and the overturning of subpostmaster convictions based on data from the Post Office’s Horizon system, the DWP announced a review of its own prosecutions of subpostmasters. The “independent assurance review”, as it was described by the DWP, will look at around 100 prosecutions between 1996 and 2018.

On 27 February 2025, the review was first announced. Speaking on behalf of the government in the House of Lords at the time, Peer Maggie Jones, in response to a question from fellow peer Prem Sikka, said: “My noble friend Lord Sikka raised a question about the DWP convictions. I can assure him that the minister for transformation is looking into this, a review is being established, and I hope to provide more information about that.”

But this week, 17 months later, in answer to a freedom of information (FOI) request by campaigner and former subpostmaster Tim McCormack, the DWP said it has not chosen the person to review the cases: “The process of [reviewer’s] appointment is still underway.”

It said, once agreed,  the name of the independent reviewer will be announced in a ministerial statement. Furthermore, the DWP admitted that the terms of reference of the review “are not yet finalised”.

In the FOI response, it said: “[They] remain subject to stakeholder engagement and ministerial clearance. We do not yet have a confirmed publication date, but publication is expected once that process has been completed.”

A DWP spokespersomn said: The process of appointing an Independent Reviewer is ongoing. A Direct Ministerial Appointment can’t be made until the new Prime Minister has had the opportunity to consider. Details of this appointment as well as a timeline of the review will be set out in due course."

In reaction to the DWP’s admission that the review has not yet started, Sikka told Computer Weekly: “It is disgraceful that after 17 months of promises nothing has been done. The promised review has not begun, and no reviewer has been appointed. The government lethargy is prolonging the pain and misery of postmasters and their families. Justice delayed is justice denied. Something is very wrong at the heart of the government.”

Fellow peer and long-time campaigner for justice for subpostmasters affected in the Post Office scandal, James Arbuthnot, told Computer Weekly: “It is clear that the DWP is dragging its feet.”

He added that the department’s approach mirrors that of earlier government efforts to avoid investigating allegations over the Post Office Horizon system: “It doesn’t see the need for this investigation, much like the Post Office didn’t see the need to look into Horizon. It is also trying to limit its scope and effectiveness as much as it can, much like the government tried to limit the scope and effectiveness of the public inquiry Boris Johnson promised, which civil servants tried to reduce to a ‘review’.” 

He said the DWP’s advertisement for a reviewer – whose work is to be limited to 30 days and who won’t look at individual cases – “makes the job pointless” and that “it’s time for Parliament to step in”, cadding: “I have discussed this with Lord Sikka and I expect we shall be working together on it.”

Neil Hudgell, lawyer at Hudgell Solicitors, which represents hundreds of Post Office scandal victims, said: “It beggars belief that this review has not started. Not much has happened since this time last year, other than attempts by DWP to limit its reach and water down any meaningful investigation. Only a full review of all cases on their own merits will do and it needs to start now and move at speed.”

Around 100 subpostmasters and staff were prosecuted by the DWP with support from the Post Office. The DWP said it has recovered material and reviewed cases, but has so far has not found evidence that Horizon data was used by it to prosecute subpostmasters or branch staff.

In January, Hudgell told Computer Weekly that his law firm is pursuing its own investigations on behalf of clients, and already had “a couple of cases lined up” to send to the CCRC.

“We’ve unearthed some interesting things that we think impact the safety of convictions, so we’re not waiting around on DWP themselves,” said Hudgell. “Someone needs to lean on the DWP, because it’s not good enough. [The longer it takes,] the more suspicion subpostmasters have that there’s something to hide.”

Polluted prosecutions

Focus turned on the DWP after the Post Office Horizon controversy hit the mainstream following the ITV drama about the scandal, which saw hundreds of subpostmasters wrongly prosecuted following account shortfalls.

These discrepancies were caused by errors in the Post Office’s Horizon system used in branches and effected thousands of subpostmasters. More than 700 subpostmaster convictions, which were based on data from Horizon, were overturned en masse through an act of Parliament in May 2024.

The DWP worked with the Post Office on its subpostmaster prosecutions, and it has emerged that prosecutions of people using various systems at Post Office branches could also be flawed. The CCRC now refers to cases based on multiple technologies as “pre-Horizon appeals”, such is the variety of systems involved.

The DWP said prosecutions were related to fraudulent activity on the DWP payment mechanisms such as order book fraud, but Hudgell has stated that “all prosecutions involving the Post Office are polluted and need to be looked at”.

In an update, a DWP spokesperson told Computer Weekly: “We announced an independent assurance review where Post Office members of staff were prosecuted by the Department for welfare-related fraud. Over the past few years, we have taken comprehensive steps to recover material and review all relevant cases. To date, no documentation has been identified to show that Horizon data was essential to any DWP prosecutions.”

The DWP said it will not review criminal convictions.

title: Russian APT Laundry Bear perfects zero-click phishing attack
raw_text:
An emerging threat actor linked with confidence to the Russian state is targeting Western organisations with a novel zero-click phishing attack technique designed to compromise email platforms and gain persistent access to its target networks.

Flagged by the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), alongside its Five Eyes partners and sister agencies from across Europe, the new operation has been given the name Laundry Bear, and has successfully stolen sensitive data from multiple targets in sectors such as defence, education, energy, government, law enforcement, media and non-governmental organisations (NGOs).

The advanced persistent threat (APT) group has likely been around since 2024, and has developed a zero-click exploit termed beehive or Ulej that specifically targets Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software. The NCSC said this technique was initially tested against Ukrainian targets prior to being turned against Western organisations, which is “indicative of espionage” and means Laundry Bear is “almost certainly” acting with Moscow’s support.

“This phishing campaign demonstrates how hostile actors will ruthlessly adapt techniques and exploit vulnerable technology in pursuit of their aims to steal sensitive information from Western organisations,” said NCSC chief operating officer Beth Hopkins.

“With our international partners, we strongly encourage organisations to familiarise themselves with the zero-click techniques described in the advisory which could be used against other platforms, and act on the mitigation advice. 

“We will continue to call out malicious cyber activity supported by the Russian state and urge everyone to follow NCSC guidance to raise resilience, including steps to strengthen online account security.” 

Busy bees

The background to Laundry Bear’s campaign dates back to May 2025 when the Dutch authorities warned of a cluster of malicious activity targeting Microsoft Exchange and abusing legitimate application programming interfaces (APIs) to exfiltrate bulk data. At this stage ,the group appeared to be using a malicious website masquerading as a European Defence and Security Summit registration portal.

However, from around July 2025, Laundry Bear shifted to a far more technical phishing method with its custom-developed beehive technique – technical analysis conducted by the NCSC suggests that artificial intelligence (AI) tools were used in the generation of a simple codebase for this purpose.

Unlike the Microsoft campaign, beehive enables Laundry Bear to gain sustained access to its target’s emails with no input from the user. More usually, a victim must click a link or open a file to enable this kind of access but in this instance, they only have to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of ZCS’ webmail service in order to be compromised.

Beehive specifically targets a flaw tracked as CVE-2025-66376, a stored cross-site-scripting (XSS) vulnerability in ZCS’ classic user interface that allows attackers to abuse cascading style sheets (CSS) @import directives in email HTML.

Zimbra patched this flaw in November 2025 and the NCSC is urging any users that have not updated to immediately patch it and conduct urgent network monitoring.

The NCSC warned that while CVE-2025-66376 specifically exists in ZCS, the beehive technique itself could be readily adapted to exploit other vulnerabilities. It added that as more organisations update their ZCS instances, Laundry Bear would very likely look to target other email systems as the pool of potential victims empties out.

Huntress senior manager of security operations Dray Agha said: “These exploits are a worst-case scenario for defenders because it is a zero-click attack, meaning simply viewing the email in a vulnerable client triggers the compromise. This completely bypasses traditional employee security training and gives state-backed hackers a silent, invisible backdoor into sensitive communications without the victim ever making a mistake.

“This is why defence-in-depth is advised, as where the human security layer is porous, the technical defensive layer can step in. Organisations shouldn’t just longer rely on their staff acting as a human firewall. Rapid software patching, coupled with layered technical defences, is the only reliable safety net against modern state-sponsored threats.”

title: CW@60: The mirror and the machine - three decades on the frontlines of the tech revolution
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

For those of us working in IT, our industry history is not something you read about - it is something we have lived.

That experience mirrors my own journey running technology services companies, spanning three distinct eras of rapid change. If you want to understand how we got here, you only have to look at how Computer Weekly has adapted.

Launched in 1966 to cover the dawn of business mainframes, its pages grew up alongside our industry. As we shifted our focus from raw technical implementation to digital transformation, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence (AI), Computer Weekly’s editorial lens shifted right along with us.

But what I admire most about the publication and what resonates with anyone who has had to manage complex tech programmes is that the team never just reported on the technology. Through the relentless, investigative journalism of individuals like Tony Collins and Karl Flinders, they tackled the human and societal impact of technology long before the mainstream media even noticed.

For me, that’s the real legacy - technology isn't just about the device, data element or language model but also about the truthful impact of the outcome behind the implementation.

Heavy iron

When I first entered the technology sector 30 years ago, the landscape was unrecognisable by today’s standards. We were firmly entrenched in what I consider to be the first modern era of business computing - the era of infrastructure and “heavy iron”.

In the mid-1990s, the ghost of the mainframe still lingered, and the client-server revolution was hitting its stride. Back then, an IT services provider was essentially an engineering guild. We spoke in the tactile language of hardware developments, localised networks, and monolithic software deployments. If you wanted to scale a business, you didn't click a button on a digital dashboard - you literally poured concrete for a new server room, ran miles of copper cabling, and prayed the mechanical and electrical parts wouldn’t fail.

“The technology story is always, fundamentally, a human-interest story. And for those of us steering technology services companies, that remains our highest directive”

Sam Kingston, Zenitech

During those early years, Computer Weekly was our trade bible. It sat on every workbench and executive’s desk. In that first era, the publication mirrored an obsession with technical execution. Its pages were filled with architectural diagrams, programming debates, and deep dives into raw processing power. To the outside world, IT was a mysterious back-room function - a cost centre managed by introverted specialists who spoke a dialect of acronyms. We were the builders, and the trade press reflected our obsession.

Then came the second era, a seismic shift that rolled in with the new millennium - the era of strategy and integration.

Almost overnight, the conversation shifted from how the technology worked, to what the technology could do for the bottom line. This was the dawn of true digital transformation.

Business outcomes

As an executive running a services company, my role fundamentally changed. I was no longer just selling engineering capacity - I was selling business outcomes. We began dismantling the very silos we had spent the previous decade building, replacing them with enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, global supply chain integrations, and eventually, the early iterations of cloud computing.

As our corporate responsibilities grew, Computer Weekly evolved right alongside us. The editorial tone matured from tactical to strategic. The cover stories were no longer just about the fastest processor - they were about leadership challenges, CIO alignments, and the macroeconomic impact of IT.

It was during this second era that a critical realisation dawned on the industry - one that both the publication and the tech industry experienced simultaneously. Technology was becoming too powerful, and too deeply embedded in public life, to be left ungoverned. When big IT projects failed, they no longer just inconvenienced a single department - they disrupted the total enterprise, government agencies, halted public services, and cost shareholders and taxpayers millions.

This brings us to the third, and current era – that of pervasive smart tech and ethical accountability debates.

Today, running a technology services firm means operating at the tipping point of human and smart tech control. We are building the architectures for AI, navigating the asymmetric warfare of modern cyber security, and managing cloud infrastructures which hold the collective data of society. Tech is no longer a tool used by a business - tech is the business.

Yet, as the capabilities of our systems have scaled exponentially, so have the stakes of their failure. And this is exactly where the paths of corporate IT and investigative journalism converge into something profoundly impactful.

Bloodhound instincts

To the general public, Computer Weekly might seem like an esoteric industry journal. However, to those who understand the history of British investigative journalism, it represents something far more formidable.

While mainstream media outlets were chasing fleeting political scandals, Computer Weekly journalists were doing the heavy lifting on the tech beat. They possessed a tenacious, bloodhound instinct to seek out and report stories that national newspapers were too slow, too confused, or too reluctant to follow.

The most defining testament to this is the decades-long, relentless coverage of the Post Office Horizon IT scandal which is widely regarded as one of the greatest miscarriages of justice in British history.

Long before television dramas brought the story into the public consciousness, it was Computer Weekly who first broke the story in 2009. They listened to the subpostmasters when the institution ignored them. They understood, with technical precision, that software is not infallible, and that hiding behind a faulty computer system to ruin innocent lives is a profound ethical failure.

As an IT executive, that specific event is not merely a historical footnote - it is a cautionary tale that informs how we should lead today.

Relentless change

When you spend 30 years watching an industry grow from mainframes to machine learning, you lose your naivety. You realise that our job as technology leaders is not just to deploy the latest cutting-edge platform or chase the highest margin. Our job is to ensure that we build systems resilient enough to survive real-world failure and insulate our clients from catastrophic operational and legal risk.

Looking back across three decades of rapid, relentless change, the technology has changed beyond recognition. The copper wires have become invisible cloud networks, and the programming scripts are now written by algorithms. But the human element remains completely unchanged.

Computer Weekly succeeded because it realised early on that the technology story is always, fundamentally, a human-interest story. And for those of us steering technology services companies through this third era, that remains our highest directive - to build with integrity, to manage with strategy, and to appreciate the real-world implications of the code we deploy.

Sam Kingston is CEO at Zenitech.

title: MI5 and PSNI ordered to pay damages to BBC journalist Vincent Kearney over unlawful surveillance
raw_text:
A court has ordered the Security Service and the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) to pay damages to a former BBC journalist for unlawfully accessing his phone data.

The PSNI and MI5 have been ordered to pay Vincent Kearney damages of £10,000 each for accessing his communications data in an attempt to identify his confidential journalistic sources.

The case represents the first time MI5 has been ordered to pay damages for conducting unlawful surveillance.

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal today identified seven occasions between 2006 and 2017 where authorisations were issued to access Kearney’s phone data that were disproportionate and not in accordance with the law.

Kearney and the BBC brought the case in 2024 after learning that his phone data had been accessed from evidence that emerged from a separate case brought by journalists Barry McCaffrey and Trevor Birney against the PSNI.

Victory for journalists

Vincent Kearney, currently northern editor at RTÉ, was home affairs correspondent for BBC Northern Ireland at the time of the surveillance.

“This is a tremendous victory for journalism and an affirmation of the duty and legal rights of journalists to protect sources,” he said after today’s judgment.

“The award of damages against MI5 is particularly significant as it is the first time the IPT has taken such action, and the first time the security service has been ordered to pay damages to a journalist,” said Kearney.

“The court has ruled that the PSNI and MI5 broke the law when they interfered with my communications data over a period of many years in efforts to identify confidential sources,” he added.

According to the IPT judgment, any measures taken that interfere with the confidentiality of a journalist’s sources must be “justified by an overriding requirement in the public interest” and any authorisation to do so must be first reviewed by a judge or another independent body.

MI5 unlawfully accessed phone data

The court found that MI5 first applied for billing data, and details of phone numbers that had been in contact with Kearney, in 2006. MI5’s applications failed to identify Kearney as a journalist and failed to state their purpose was to identify his journalistic sources, the court found.

MI5 said it had acted in “good faith” by following the codes of practice at the time, but admitted it had breached Kearney’s rights to privacy and freedom of expression, which protects confidential journalistic sources under the European Convention on Human Rights.

In 2009, Kearney was again subject to surveillance after he received a call from an individual claiming to be from the Continuity IRA claiming responsibility for the murder of PC Stephen Carroll, which he notified to the PSNI.

The PSNI made applications for the BBC and Kearney’s phone data, but failed to ask whether there was an “overriding requirement in the public” interest to interfere with the confidentiality of Kearney’s journalistic sources.

MPS obtained geographic data about Kearney

In 2011, the PSNI commissioned the Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) to investigate Kearney following his work on a BBC Spotlight programme that reported the Office of the Police Ombudsman for Northern Ireland had been compromised.

Under Operation Erewhon, the MPS obtained Kearney’s communications data for over three months, which included incoming and outgoing calls, cell site data, and data about Kearney’s geographic movements.

“We have seen nothing to suggest that there was any overriding public interest remotely sufficient to justify either this intrusion or the wide interference, for such an extended period, with the confidentiality of his journalistic sources,” the court found.

In 2013, the PSNI applied for Kearney’s phone data as part of Operation Samarium, an investigation into allegations that a senior PSNI manager had received corrupt payments.

The PSNI made two applications which identified Kearney as a journalist, but failed to establish any justification, let alone an “overriding requirement” for obtaining such a large quantity of Kearney’s phone data. One of the applications falsely identified Kearney as a suspect in the investigation.

A PSNI investigation in 2014, dubbed Operation Basanti, made four applications to obtain phone data relating to an individual suspected of being a journalistic source for Kearney.

Although the applications made it clear that Kearney was a journalist, they did not address the legal significance of that, and failed to apply the correct legal tests before authorising the operation.

Documentary

In 2017, the PSNI commissioned Durham Constabulary to investigate alleged leaks following the broadcast of the documentary, No stone unturned, which revealed allegations of police collusion into the murders of six innocent Catholics at Loughinisland in 1984.

Under Operation Yurta, Durham obtained a spreadsheet of communications data relating to Kearney originally obtained by the MPS in 2012 during Operation Erewhon.

The MPS accepted that it breached Kearney’s rights by obtaining and storing Kearney’s communications data and providing parts of the data to Durham Constabulary.

The IPT found that the retention and use of Kearney’s and the BBC’s data was also unlawful because it was not proportionate nor in accordance with the law.

In 2024, the IPT found that Belfast journalists Barry McCaffrey and Trevor Birney were unlawfully placed under surveillance by two UK police forces that spied on their phone communications and on their suspected confidential sources.

The journalists were targeted after they produced a documentary exposing police collusion in the murders of six innocent Catholics watching a football match in Loughinisland in 1994.

Information disclosed in their case suggested other journalists, including Kearney, had been subject to surveillance.

Agencies not above the law

Kearney said the fact that the court decided to award damages reflects the seriousness of the case, including the impact of Kearney personally and the trust that sources can place in the confidentiality of their communications with him.

“It is important that agencies charged with upholding the law know that they are not above the law and will be held to account,” he said.

A BBC spokesperson said the issues raised by this case were a matter of grave concern, not just to the BBC, but to wider society.

“What happened in this instance was wrong and must never be repeated,” said the spokesperson. “It caused harm to a journalist, jeopardised trust and threatened the safeguards on which public interest journalism depends, and has a right to expect.”

Commenting on the judgment, the chief constable of the PSNI, Jon Boutcher, said: “I accept the Investigatory Powers Tribunal’s judgment that the PSNI authorisations were not in accordance with the law and were disproportionate.”

He said that significant changes to practice and policy had been made since these incidents occurred. These included the role of the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office in independently authorising communications data requests and scrutiny of Judicial Commissioners of requests to access communications relating to journalists.

February 2026

Police created ‘intelligence profile’ of BBC journalist subject to phone surveillance: Police and MI5 conducted seven unlawful operations to obtain phone data relating to former BBC journalist Vincent Kearney, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal heard today.

November 2025

MI5 made multiple applications for phone data to identify BBC journalist’s sources: MI5 discloses it made and authorised unlawful ‘sequential applications’ for Vincent Kearney’s phone data during his time at the BBC, but will neither confirm nor deny whether it undertook further ‘lawful’ surveillance of BBC journalists.

September 2025

Northern Ireland police kept inspectors in dark over surveillance of journalists: The Police Service of Northern Ireland failed to inform the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office about surveillance operations against journalists during annual inspections.

December 2025

Tribunal criticises PSNI and Met Police for spying operation to identify journalists’ sources: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has criticised the Police Service of Northern Ireland and the Metropolitan Police for unlawfully spying on journalists.

title: Digital government services increase accessibility gap
raw_text:
Around 20% of people in the UK cannot use digital government services without assistance, according to research.

The study from the Digital Poverty Alliance and Cognizant found that digital services are, in many cases, being build for users with the perfect conditions for accessibility, perpetuating the digital divide.

Elizabeth Anderson, CEO of Digital Poverty Alliance, commented: “As more government services move online, it is vital that digital transformation does not come at the expense of inclusion. For the 19 million people in the UK currently experiencing digital exclusion, this creates a real risk of new barriers to accessing essential services.

“The shift toward digital-only systems risks leaving vulnerable groups behind particularly those without reliable internet access, suitable devices or the confidence to navigate complex online platforms.

“Services must be designed to meet people where they are – with fewer bugs, more intuitive design and greater support funded as a part of the service. At the same time, if government is relying on informal networks of local community groups to provide support, this must be sustainably funded and supported with proper training for support workers.”

The world is increasingly moving towards digital, utilising technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), but there are still a large number of people in the UK who are unable to use digital, including those with disabilities or those from lower-income backgrounds, who in many cases will need to access certain services the UK government is increasingly digitising.

The Digital Poverty Alliance and Cognizant focused on digital services such as organising Universal Credit and Pension Credit, managing identity documents and driving licences, and applying for visas or schools. When trying to use these systems, 60% of adults found it difficult to log in, and a quarter found it difficult to use and navigate these systems.

The digital divide plays a role in these challenges, with 10% of adults not having reliable internet access to use digital government systems, while 10% also can only access the internet through a phone, which are not the ideal devices for accessing these services.

Many claimed they must use limited mobile data or have poor signal in their homes, and do not want to use services involving their personal data in public, while others say a large screen and keyboard are frequently required for tasks such as filling in forms, which are technologies they do not have access to.

When looking at younger adults, difficulty accessing and navigating digital government services increased to 40%, likely due to their default format for accessing and using the internet being mobile phones.

More than half of those struggling opted to phone a government helpline, 60% of which found it helpful – but others said there were long waiting times and were often then redirected back to digital channels. Almost a quarter claimed they wouldn’t have been able to use online government services without the help of friends, families or charities.

Yatin Mahandru, UK&I head of public sector and health at Cognizant, urged the government and other organisations not to default to “digital only” when developing online services.

He said: “The answer isn’t to slow transformation down, it’s to design it around how citizens actually live, on the devices they really use, with assisted and human support built in from the start across citizen journeys, rather than bolted on at the end.

“Done well, modern service design and AI can make government services dramatically simpler, more accessible and more impactful for everyone. The leaders who get this right will measure success not by how many services they move online, but by how many people they reach.”

title: Alphabet borrows $100bn to pay for AI investments
raw_text:
Alphabet, the parent company of Google, has reported revenue for the second quarter of 2026 of £120bn, an increase of 24%, with Google Cloud experiencing “accelerated” growth.

The Google Cloud Platform posted revenue of almost $25bn, an 82% increase from the previous year, driven by demand for artificial intelligence (AI). But the company’s capital expenditure (CapEx) during the quarter was $44.bn, with the vast majority of that being spent on technical infrastructure to support the company’s investments in AI.

Of the $45.9bn in costs incurred during the quarter, it spent $18.2bn on research and development.

CEO Sundar Pichai said: “One of the strongest parts of our growth comes from the rapid adoption of our Gemini Enterprise platform. It is differentiated with easy-to-use tools to build agents and automate processes, connectivity to enterprise systems, cost management and governance tools.

“Gemini is transforming how millions of businesses use AI to build custom agents, automate processes, improve cyber security, manage customer relationships, streamline data analytics, collaborate effectively and more,” he said. “All of this momentum is driving growth in our paid token usage.”

Chief financial officer Anat Ashkenazi said: “Approximately 60% of our investment in technical infrastructure this quarter was in servers, and 40% was in datacentres and networking equipment.”

She said the company has revised its full-year 2026 CapEx guidance range to $195-205bn, up from its previous estimate of $180-190bn. “The increase in the range is primarily due to an acceleration in the delivery of capacity to meet growing demand,” said Ashkenazi. “As we previously shared, we continue to expect our CapEx to increase significantly in 2027.”

She said the increase in spending would put pressure on Alphabet’s profit and loss account in the form of higher depreciation expense and related datacentre operations costs. When questioned about the rise in CapEx, Ashkenazi said: “We take a multi-year view at what the needs are, as well as focus on next year in the near term and build aggressively to meet those demands.”

She said the company has also expanded its debt portfolio “quite significantly over the past 12 months”. This has grown from $16bn to $100bn.

Along with running AI inference and machine learning workloads for its cloud customers, agentic AI is one of the areas the company has begun expanding into.

Speaking about agentic AI in e-commerce, Philipp Schindler, chief business officer, used his prepared remarks during the earnings call to talk about agent-to-agent e-commerce. He said Alphabet has been running with a number of retailers, including Target, and described the open-source Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) as “the new standard for agentic commerce”.

“Merchants are rapidly adopting UCP,” said Schindler. “We also announced Universal Cart, allowing shoppers to add to items from different retailers across Google surfaces and buy in a single checkout.”

Commenting on the Alphabet results, Forrester vice-president and research director Emily Collins said: “The results suggest Google is successfully using AI to deepen engagement while expanding its role across product discovery, shopping and commerce. As AI reshapes digital experiences, Google is positioning itself to monetise consumer intent across the entire customer journey.”
